passages.reading88: For centuries, the Silk Road served as far more than a conduit for commodities; it was a vibrant artery through which ideas, beliefs and technologies flowed between civilisations. Merchants traversing its (1)________ terrain, which included scorching deserts, treacherous mountain passes and desolate steppes, carried not merely silk and spices but also philosophies that would profoundly reshape the societies they touched. The exchange was remarkably (2)________. Buddhism journeyed eastward from India into China, while papermaking techniques gradually migrated westward, eventually transforming scholarship in the Islamic world and Europe. Such cross-pollination fostered a cosmopolitan ethos in bustling entrepo ts like Samarkand and Kashgar, where polyglot traders haggled in myriad tongues. Yet the route was not without its perils. Brigands lay in wait for (3)________ caravans, and the vicissitudes of politics could abruptly sever vital links. The collapse of a single empire often precipitated a decline in commerce across vast regions, illustrating how interdependent these far-flung economies had become. Historians caution against romanticising this era, noting that disease, too, travelled along these pathways; the Black Death is widely believed to have spread partly through such networks. Nonetheless, the Silk Road's legacy remains (4)________. It demonstrates that human progress has seldom been the achievement of isolated societies but rather the fruit of sustained interaction. In today's increasingly insular  political  climate,  this lesson acquires fresh  (5)________. Nations contemplating a retreat behind protectionist barriers would do well to remember that prosperity has historically flourished where borders were porous and minds were receptive.
